sales-basics-1: Selling follows a sequence of steps, whatever is sold, and I wrote the sale down as a script so that a new salesman could learn it. The textbook's seven steps are a modern version of the same idea. Write them in your own words and say what happens in each. Then test each step for a trick: would the buyer be comfortable reading your page? The Primer itself warned against making a merchant feel he was being sold, and a process is worth having only if it serves the buyer.

Needs are essentials, wants improve life, and emotion pushes both. Learn to tell a reason that is useful from one that is pleasurable, and ask which is driving this buyer. I gave every salesman a territory and asked for a daily record, because I wanted to know who bought and why. Write down the last three things you bought and sort each reason. Then think how you would sell to each of those buyers, and how you would not.

A consumer buys for a household, and a business buys to produce, resell or run an organisation. The buying group in a business can have several people, each with a different concern. Identify who in a company decides, who uses and who pays. Keep a record of each contact. A salesman who knows the group before he calls spends less time in the wrong room.

The business buying process has stages: recognise the need, define it, set specifications, search, ask for proposals, evaluate, decide, and judge afterwards. Features, advantages and benefits turn a product into a reason. State each benefit in the buyer's terms and check that it is true. I told salesmen to show sincerity and sympathy for the buyer's business, and a benefit stated without those is only a claim.

If you supply food or goods to the public from home, you are a business under the law, and you must meet its rules. Registering and controlling hazards is part of selling honestly. Read this lesson as the rules that stand behind the script. Write what you must do before your first sale and who you must tell. When the rule is specific, follow it; when it is not, ask.
sales-basics-2: Prospecting comes first, because you cannot sell to people you have not identified. A lead is a name, and a prospect is a lead that fits. The funnel shows how many fall away at each step. I gave each salesman a territory so that nobody wandered, and you should write an ideal customer profile in one paragraph. Count the leads you have today and the prospects among them.

The best sources depend on your ideal customer, so ask where that person looks for information. List ten sources and choose the three that fit. A cold call can be respectful if it is brief, honest and ready to end. I wrote down what to say, but never to force. Write the first thirty seconds of a call you would be glad to receive.

Not every lead is worth a presentation. Qualify: is the person ready, willing and able to buy? Five questions will tell you. It is kind to the buyer as well as to you to stop when the answer is no. I asked for a daily record of calls and results, and you should record why you qualified a lead in or out.

Good records turn prospecting into a system. A customer relationship record keeps each contact, the date and the next step. Keep only what you need, and treat personal details with care. I asked for reports every day, and the habit is what matters, not the machine. Set up a simple sheet, fill it in each evening, and review it on Friday.
sales-basics-3: The preapproach is finding out about a prospect before you contact them. Researching shows you care and lets you sell adaptively. Fill in a precall worksheet: who they are, what they do, what they might need. Find one thing that really interests you. Genuine interest is the first of the six ways to make people like you, and it cannot be faked for long. Write what you learned and what you still do not know.

Great salespeople solve rather than sell. The same camera is a different solution for a teenager and for a grandmother. Write a general benefit statement and a specific one, and set a SMART objective for the call. Talk in terms of the other person's interest. Test each statement: is it true of this person's situation? If not, cut it.

The approach is your first contact, and you are not selling yet. You are introducing yourself and opening the way. Use the six Cs to plan it, and choose phone, email or a visit by what suits the person. Smile, use their name, and listen. Check where the textbook and the law differ on contact, and follow the law. Practise the first thirty seconds aloud.

Choose an approach that fits the situation and the customer, and mix them. Gatekeepers are doing their job, so be courteous and clear. Rejection is part of the work, and it is information. Don't criticise, condemn or complain, whatever the answer. Log each rejection with the reason you were given, and thank the person.
sales-basics-4: The presentation is where the qualifying and the planning pay off. Prepare the logistics, rehearse, and plan how to adapt. Think from the customer's standpoint: what will they ask, what will they need to see? I treated the window as a craft, and a presentation deserves the same care. Write the three questions the buyer is most likely to ask, and your answers.

SPIN uses four kinds of question in order: situation, problem, implication and need-payoff. Ask more than you tell, and let the buyer talk. The first contact decides the goodwill, so listen well. Write one question of each kind for your own offer, and role-play them. Check that you are not leading the buyer to an answer you chose in advance.

A sales presentation has five steps: build rapport, make a general benefit statement, a specific one, present, then close and recap. Ask how much time you have and who is in the room. Stage the product so it can be seen and handled. Keep your statements dependable. Time your presentation and cut it to fit.

In business sales, closing often depends on whether the value outweighs the cost. Use a cost-benefit comparison and a return on investment, with the arithmetic shown. Write a proposal that a stranger could understand. Use a table of percentages, as I did in the store. Check every number twice before you send it.
sales-basics-5: An objection is a question or a hesitation, and usually it masks a request for more information. Treat it as an invitation to go on. Many nos really mean 'tell me more'. Write the five reasons people do not buy and a question for each. Prepare for the common ones before the call. Listening to an objection is part of selling for the buyer, not to the buyer.

Price deserves special care. Price is what the customer pays, and value is what they receive. Check that price is the real objection before you answer it, and repeat it as a question. Don't cut the price quickly, because it skips the value conversation. Learn the six types of objection and a response to each. Do not argue: objections thrive on opposition and die with agreement.

Closing starts at the beginning of the selling process. It is asking for the order, not trickery or pressure. Choose a close that fits the buyer and the offer, and use the buyer's own reasons. A cost close compares total cost over time, and it is honest only if the figures are. A no today is better than a no tomorrow, so ask plainly.

Negotiation is discussing an issue between parties with competing interests, and the aim is that seller, buyer and relationship all gain. Know what you can give and what you cannot. Follow up after the sale, to check that the buyer is satisfied. Keep your word. Record what you agreed, and send it in writing.
sales-basics-6: Ethics are the moral principles that define right and wrong, and a salesperson meets the customer face to face. My firm followed up a rumour about a supplier and acted on what it found, and it took years and cost trade. Spot the dilemma in a sale and choose the honest response. Write a case from your own experience, what you did and what it cost. Honesty is a habit you build in small cases.

Consumer law protects buyers against practices that mislead, pressure or distort the buying decision. Check the tactics from earlier modules against it. A practice that tricks the buyer is unfair even if it works. Write which of the tactics you would remove from your script and why. Keep your claims to what you can show.

Direct marketing by phone or electronic mail is regulated, and you must know who you may contact. Check the rules for live calls, emails and texts, and for the UK and Ireland separately. When in doubt, don't. Write your rule for who you may contact, and keep the evidence of consent. Ask the person if you may follow up.

Good records support honest, lawful selling. If you can identify a person from a contact detail, it is personal data. Tell people who you are and why you hold their details. Write your personal code in five lines and a test for each. Review it each year. A code you have never tested is a hope.
sales-basics-cap: The brief is a one-page call plan that covers every step of the selling process, with a five-minute role-play. Choose something you could genuinely sell and a real or realistic prospect. Prepare as I would: genuine interest, a worksheet, a benefit in their terms. Smile, use their name, and plan to listen. Write the plan and read it as the buyer would.

Role-play the call with a partner who raises at least two objections. Record it if you both agree, and say why. Avoid the argument, show respect for opinions, and admit mistakes at once. Score the call against the rubric and write what you would change. Ask your partner whether you were sincere. Keep only the lines you would say to a friend.
